title: Applications of Electrostatics
lead: Everything the chapter has built, the excess charge a conductor carries on its outside surface, the points where that charge concentrates, the field a charge makes and the force that field exerts on another charge, is put to work in this section. A Van de Graaff generator, a copy machine, a laser printer, an ink jet printer and the precipitator that takes the smoke out of a power plant’s stack gas are all the same physics arranged differently, and the section ends with the strategy for solving an electrostatics problem and with a worked example that joins the electric force to Newton’s laws.
objectives: Name several real-world applications of the study of electrostatics.
summary_html:
• Electrostatics is the study of electric fields in static equilibrium.
  • In addition to research using equipment such as a Van de Graaff generator, many practical applications of electrostatics exist, including photocopiers, laser printers, ink-jet printers and electrostatic air filters.

figures.original_caption: Schematic of Van de Graaff generator. A battery (A) supplies excess positive charge to a pointed conductor, the points of which spray the charge onto a moving insulating belt near the bottom. The pointed conductor (B) on top in the large sphere picks up the charge. (The induced electric field at the points is so large that it removes the charge from the belt.) This can be done because the charge does not remain inside the conducting sphere but moves to its outside surface. An ion source inside the sphere produces positive ions, which are accelerated away from the positive sphere to high velocities.

(Figure 18.35) Xerography is a dry copying process based on electrostatics. The major steps in the process are the charging of the photoconducting drum, transfer of an image creating a positive charge duplicate, attraction of toner to the charged parts of the drum, and transfer of toner to the paper. Not shown are heat treatment of the paper and cleansing of the drum for the next copy. (Figure 18.36) In a laser printer, a laser beam is scanned across a photoconducting drum, leaving a positive charge image. The other steps for charging the drum and transferring the image to paper are the same as in xerography. Laser light can be very precisely controlled, enabling laser printers to produce high-quality images.

The nozzle of an ink-jet printer produces small ink droplets, which are sprayed with electrostatic charge. Various computer-driven devices are then used to direct the droplets to the correct positions on a page.

(a) Schematic of an electrostatic precipitator. Air is passed through grids of opposite charge. The first grid charges airborne particles, while the second attracts and collects them. (b) The dramatic effect of electrostatic precipitators is seen by the absence of smoke from this power plant. (credit: Cmdalgleish, Wikimedia Commons)

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the direction and magnitude of an electric field that supports the weight of a free electron near the surface of Earth? (b) Discuss what the small value for this field implies regarding the relative strength of the gravitational and electrostatic forces.

answer.hint: The field must exert an upward force equal to the weight of the electron, so set $\kq\kEf$ equal to $m\kg$ with the mass of the electron and the magnitude of its charge. The electron is negative, so the force on it is opposite to the field.
answer.solution: (a) $5.58 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N/C}$ (b) the coulomb force is extraordinarily stronger than gravity

exercises.prompt: Earth has a net charge that produces an electric field of approximately 150 N/C downward at its surface. (a) What is the magnitude and sign of the excess charge, noting the electric field of a conducting sphere is equivalent to a point charge at its center? (b) What acceleration will the field produce on a free electron near Earth’s surface? (c) What mass object with a single extra electron will have its weight supported by this field?

parts.hint: Turn the field of a point charge around to give the charge, with the radius of Earth as the distance. A field that points downward, toward the center, belongs to a negative charge.
The force on the electron is the magnitude of its charge times the field, and the acceleration follows from Newton’s second law with the mass of the electron.
Set the electric force on one elementary charge equal to the weight $m\kg$ and solve for the mass.

exercises.prompt: What can you say about two charges $\kqone$ and $\kqtwo$, if the electric field one-fourth of the way from $\kqone$ to $\kqtwo$ is zero?

answer.solution: The charge $\kqtwo$ is 9 times greater than $\kqone$.

exercises.prompt: A frictionless circular track with a diameter of 4.00 m has two spheres of 10.0 kg each anchored very near it. The track is oriented with a diameter along the x-axis. The anchored spheres are just outside the track. One of the anchored spheres is just left of the origin at a distance of $1.00 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$ from it, and the other is on the x-axis just right of the track at a distance of $1.00 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$ past $(4,0)$. Each sphere carries a charge of $2.00 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{C}$. (Note: The slight distance from the track is so the particles cannot collide, and does not enter into the calculations for three significant figures.) (a) A third sphere has a mass of 10.00 kg and carries a charge of $-1.00 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{C}$. It is free to move on the track. It is initially placed an equal length from the two anchored spheres at $(2.00,2.00)$. What is the total force on the third sphere? (Be certain to include gravity between the spheres.) (b) Will the third sphere move? (c) Label the first two spheres A and B, and the movable sphere C. Now start sphere C at $(1.00,2.00)$. What are the forces on sphere C? (d) Will sphere C now move? (e) If it does, where will it stop moving and reverse course? If it does not move, you may skip this part. (f) How many equilibrium points are there on the track at which the movable sphere will remain stationary? Where are they?

answer.solution: (a) The forces are balanced in the x-direction, so the net force is vertical. It is composed of the sum of the vertical components of the Coulomb force and the gravitational force. $F_y = -2\left(\frac{k\kqone\kqtwo}{r^2} + G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}\right)\cos 45^\circ = -4.36 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{N}$ (b) No, it is in a metastable position. Since it cannot move horizontally, it cannot traverse any part of the track. (c) $F_x = 2.60 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{N}$ and $F_y = -6.36 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{N}$, each of them the sum of the Coulomb force and the gravitational force from the two anchored spheres, resolved along the axes. (d) Yes. (e) It will reach $(1,-\sqrt{3})$ before it will change direction. (f) The metastable positions where there is no component in one direction are $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(2,2)$ and $(2,-2)$. They number 4.
